summary: 41a covers: the anonymous Sifra follows R. Yehuda (setam Sifra = R. Yehuda); Rav Chisda's ruling that kinnim (bird-pair offerings) are only designated at the moment of slaughter (first slaughtered = chatat); R. Yochanan's counter that explicit prior designation is also binding; multiple kinnim scenarios about what happens when birds die or are mixed up.

learning.ahaMoment: When the Gemara says 'the Sifra' without naming an author, it always means R. Yehuda.
learning.memoryAnchor: Setam Sifra = R. Yehuda - the quiet author behind the Torat Kohanim.
learning.learnerQuestion: Why does it matter that an unattributed ruling in the Sifra is assumed to follow R. Yehuda?
learning.coreTension: A ruling stated without a named author could in principle follow any tanna's position, leaving its halachic weight and scope ambiguous until the author is identified.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara states the general attribution rule directly, then applies it to the goat-to-Azazel provisions, fixing their authorship and thereby their legal context.

takeaway.text: When the Sifra states a ruling anonymously, the Gemara treats it as following R. Yehuda's position, a default attribution rule applied here to the goat-to-Azazel provisions.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may assume anonymous rulings are authorless or universally agreed-upon, missing that the Gemara assigns them a specific, identifiable author by a fixed convention.

display.title: Kinnim: Designated by Slaughter, Not by Intent

learning.ahaMoment: Bird pair designation is activated by the act of slaughter, not by prior intent - the event determines identity.
learning.memoryAnchor: Kinnim identity = determined at slaughter: which is cut first = that becomes the chatat; the survivor becomes the olah.
learning.learnerQuestion: When does a pair of birds (kinnim) become specifically designated as the chatat and the olah?
learning.coreTension: A woman bringing kinnim might intend from the outset which bird is which, yet Rav Chisda holds that intent alone does not fix their identity, raising the question of what actually does.
learning.coreMove: Rav Chisda rules that designation occurs only at the moment of slaughter, the first bird slaughtered for chatat becomes the chatat, while R. Yochanan counters that explicit prior naming is also binding even before slaughter, and the Gemara traces the practical fallout (replacement pairs, mixed-up scenarios) from each position.

takeaway.text: Rav Chisda rules that kinnim are designated only at the moment of slaughter, the first bird slaughtered becomes the chatat and the second the olah; R. Yochanan holds that explicit prior designation is also binding, which determines what happens if a bird dies or the pair gets mixed up before slaughter.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may assume verbal designation always fixes an offering's identity, missing Rav Chisda's distinct claim that for kinnim specifically, the act of slaughter, not stated intent, is what fixes it.

misconceptions.misconception: A pair of kinnim birds becomes specifically designated the moment the woman says 'this one is the chatat.'
misconceptions.correction: According to Rav Chisda, that statement alone does not fix the designation; the birds remain potentially either the chatat or the olah until the moment of slaughter, when the first one slaughtered becomes the chatat. R. Yochanan disagrees and holds explicit prior naming is binding even before slaughter, the two positions disagree precisely on whether the woman's statement is enough.

rashiTranslations.en: Rashi: opens - the anonymous Sifra (Torat Kohanim) is [attributed to] R. Yehuda, as stated in Sanhedrin.
Rashi: continues - this appears in the Sifra [Torat Kohanim] because the source verse is written in the book of Leviticus.
Rashi: opens - kinnim are not designated [as to] which is the olah and which is the chatat, except by either the owner's taking [at acquisition] or the priest's act [at performance].

Rashi: continues - [explaining the owner's specification:] if at acquisition he says 'this one I take for the olah, this one for the chatat,' [then beyond that point] the priest cannot change them at performance.
Rashi: continues - if the priest changed them [the designation], it is invalid; and if the owner did not specify at acquisition, [then] not [does the designation take effect].
Rashi: continues - [but if the owner] specified, even though he called them [named them], [the specification does not take effect retroactively].
Rashi: continues - [because he] specified - even though he called them by name [later], the name does not apply to them.
Rashi: continues - and the priest is able to change them [if no specification was made].
Rashi: continues - and [to prove this about the priest's power, the text says] 'and she shall take and make,' establishing the principle.
Rashi: continues - in [the section about] the young woman it is written 'and she shall take two doves or [two young pigeons].'
Rashi: continues - one for the olah and one for the chatat, and likewise in the tzaraat-afflicted person, and regarding the zav the priest shall make one a chatat and one an olah.
Rashi: continues - from this we derive [the principle] that either at the time of taking they are designated, or at the time of performance [they are designated], but not in between.
Rashi: continues - 'the priest shall make one a chatat and one an olah' - [this shows that designation occurs through the priest's act at performance].
Rashi: continues - [the text states:] either at the time of taking they are designated, or at the time of performance, but not [in between].
Rashi: continues - and the passage states [multiple times] 'she shall make' and 'the priest makes,' [showing timing of designation].
Rashi: continues - [a new issue:] since it is taught here that when the lot sanctifies [one bird], it is not [automatic that the] Name sanctifies [it].
Rashi: continues - it might enter [one's] mind that the sanctification of the Name [operates differently from the lot's sanctification].
Rashi: continues - [but the resolution is that] the sanctification of the Name [occurs] at the time of the lot's sanctification - this is the teaching.
Rashi: continues - [saying] that it is not the time of taking and not the time of performance - so we have heard [the tradition].
Rashi: continues - and therefore there is a difficulty here [in reconciling the times of designation with the lot and the Name].
Rashi: continues - that it is not the time of taking and not the time of performance, yet it is taught that it was fixed [somehow, despite these constraints].
Rashi: opens - [new case:] one impure who enters the Temple, and he is bringing a kinnim offering.
Rashi: continues - [explaining:] one who enters the Temple impure - this is regarding a chatat for Temple impurity, which is an offering that ascends and descends in wealth categories.
Rashi: continues - the poverty [offering here] is the one mentioned [in Leviticus] alongside the oath of falsehood and the oath of voice.
Rashi: continues - and there [in Leviticus] it is written 'or a soul who touches' - and we have established this in [Tractate] Shevuot [regarding] Temple impurity and holy things [desecration].
Rashi: continues - [meaning: this applies] after [the person] became impure, he entered the Temple or ate holy things.
Rashi: continues - 'and the rich man' [from the Mishnah] - and he must bring [his offering] in the category of wealth.

Rashi: continues - 'and afterwards' - [the person] divided the monies [set aside] and said 'these [birds/money] for his chatat, these for his olah,' even though there is now no obligation on him for a poor man's offering but only a rich man's offering.
Rashi: continues - in a rich man's offering there is only a chatat from a [larger] animal - when he comes before the court, the court says to him 'bring a rich man's offering.'
Rashi: continues - [explaining 'adds':] [he brings money] from his house until [reaching] the price of the animal, and brings his obligation from the monies they called 'chatat.'

Rashi: continues - 'and does not add' - [he cannot take a] chatat from an animal [using money] from the monies of the olah, because he is not able to change [or redirect] the olah-monies to get the chatat from them.
Rashi: continues - 'and there is a difficulty here' - after [he] separated [the monies], he specified [which is which], and this is neither the time of taking nor the time of performance.
Rashi: continues - yet it is taught [in the Mishnah] that it was fixed [the designation took effect].
Rashi: continues - Rav Sheshet said [a resolution], and does it seem reasonable? Did not R. Elazar say [in the name of] R. Hoshayah...
Rashi: continues - 'one impure entering the Temple' - rich man - brought a poor man's offering - he does not fulfill [his obligation].
Rashi: continues - so since he does not fulfill [it], how can the name [of 'olah'] be fixed on them [the birds], when he became rich?
Rashi: continues - [because] behold he is not obligated for the olah [after becoming rich, the offering type changed, so it cannot be the olah].
Rashi: opens - but what [can] you say [to resolve this]? Perforce there is a problem [a disruption in the teaching logic] and [we must] say that this 'afterwards' [in the Mishnah]...

Rashi: continues - [the problem is a disruption;] the teaching should [instead] be: and he said 'these for his chatat, these for his olah,' and afterwards the rich man [became rich]; this is how it should flow.

Rashi: continues - [the resolution is:] because at the time [when] he designated [the monies], an offering [that was] appropriate [to his status] existed for him, and since perforce there is a disruption, so also R. Chisda resolved it thus - he already said from the time of separation.

Rashi: continues - and here [the Mishnah] teaches: one impure [who] entered [the Temple] - poor - separated monies for his kinnim and said at the time of separation 'these for his chatat, these for his olah.'

Rashi: continues - and afterwards [he] became rich - he adds and brings his obligation by monies, [and this is as the time of taking birds, because] the designation of monies is like the time of taking of birds.
Rashi: continues - and according to R. Chaga who says one impure [who] entered the Temple - rich man - brought a poor man's offering - he fulfilled [his obligation].
Rashi: continues - and because of this it is not disrupted, and this is the resolution, since he found that this offering was acceptable to him post-facto, he can teach that it was fixed.
Rashi: continues - but what [can] you say [to explain the disruption]? Perforce it is a problem [confusion in the teaching] and [we must] say that this 'afterwards' [indicates] confusion.
Rashi: continues - [but the resolution is:] rather it should be taught that he said 'these for his chatat, these for his olah, and afterwards the rich man [designation]...'
Rashi: continues - [showing] how the problem [disruption] arises from the text; [this is] R. Sheshet's reasoning [challenge to Rav Chisda's resolution].
Rashi: continues - [explaining further:] that he already said from the time of separation, and here [the Mishnah] teaches one impure [who] entered - poor - separated monies for kinnim and said...
Rashi: continues - [from] the time of separation - and R. Chisda also so resolved it, [saying] he already said from the time of separation-time.

Rashi: continues - and here the Gemara teaches one impure [who] entered the Temple - poor man who separated monies for his kinnim, saying at the time of separation 'these for the chatat, these for the olah.'
Rashi: continues - and afterwards [he] became rich - he adds and brings his obligation by monies, [because] the designation of monies is like the time of taking of birds [for kinnim].
Rashi: continues - [reiterating:] because designation of monies is [equivalent to] the time of taking the birds themselves.

Rashi: continues - and according to R. Chaga who says one impure [who] entered the Temple - rich man - brought a poor man's offering - he fulfilled [the obligation] and [from that] it is not disrupted.
Rashi: continues - and this resolution stands, since he found that this offering was acceptable to him even post-facto, he can teach that it was fixed [the Name established it].
Rashi: concludes - [on your account] perforce it [the teaching] is disrupted [without this explanation], and [this shows the problem in Rav Sheshet's challenge].
Rashi: ends - [unresolved word at end of extended discussion].
